Lifting of Polynomial Symplectomorphisms and Deformation Quantization

Alexei Kanel-Belov ††thanks: kanel@mccme.ru Affiliation: Mathematics Department, Bar-Ilan University, Ramat-Gan, 52900, Israel Affiliation: Laboratory of Advanced Combinatorics and Network Applications, Moscow Institute of Physics and Technology, Dolgoprudny, Moscow Region, 141700, Russia    Sergey Grigoriev ††thanks: gregomaths@rambler.ru Affiliation: Department of Mechanics and Mathematics, Lomonosov Moscow State University, Vorobievy Gory, Moscow, 119898, Russia    Andrey Elishev ††thanks: elishev@phystech.edu Affiliation: Laboratory of Advanced Combinatorics and Network Applications, Moscow Institute of Physics and Technology, Dolgoprudny, Moscow Region, 141700, Russia    Wenchao Zhang ††thanks: whzecomjm@gmail.com Affiliation: Mathematics Department, Bar-Ilan University, Ramat-Gan, 52900, Israel
Abstract

We study the problem of lifting of polynomial symplectomorphisms in characteristic zero to automorphisms of the Weyl algebra by means of approximation by tame automorphisms. We utilize – and reprove – D. Anick’s fundamental result on approximation of polynomial automorphisms, adapt it to the case of symplectomorphisms, and formulate the lifting problem. The lifting problem has its origins in the context of deformation quantization of the affine space and is closely related to several major open problems in algebraic geometry and ring theory.

1 Introduction

One of the active research areas in ring theory concerns the geometry of polynomial endomorphisms – that is, endomorphisms of finitely generated associative algebras (typically over a field 𝕂\mathbb{K}) subject to a set of polynomial identities and possibly carrying other structures. Arguably, the most renowned – and notoriously difficult – open problems in this area is the Jacobian conjecture of O.-H. Keller [2], open for all N≥2N\geq 2:

Conjecture 1.1.

If 𝕂\mathbb{K} is a field of characteristic zero and φ:𝔸𝕂N→𝔸𝕂N\varphi:\mathbb{A}^{N}_{\mathbb{K}}\rightarrow\mathbb{A}^{N}_{\mathbb{K}} is a polynomial mapping with unit Jacobian:

J⁡(φ)=det⁡[∂φ⁡(xi)∂xj]=1\J(\varphi)=\Det\left[\frac{\partial\varphi(x_{i})}{\partial x_{j}}\right]=1

then φ\varphi is invertible (and the inverse is also a polynomial mapping).

Recently, Tsuchimoto [6], and independently Kanel-Belov and Kontsevich [4], found a deep connection between the Jacobian conjecture and a celebrated conjecture of Dixmier [1] on endomorphisms of the Weyl algebra, which is stated as follows:

Conjecture 1.2.

Any endomorphism ϕ\phi of the nn-th Weyl algebra Wn​(𝕂)W_{n}(\mathbb{K}) in characteristic zero is invertible.

The correspondence between the two open problems, in the case of algebraically closed 𝕂\mathbb{K}, is based on the existence of a composition-preserving map

End⁡Wn​(𝕂)→End⁡𝕂⁡[x1,…,x2​n]\End W_{n}(\mathbb{K})\rightarrow\End\mathbb{K}[x_{1},\ldots,x_{2n}]

which is a homomorphism for the corresponding automorphism groups. Furthermore, the mappings that belong to the image of this homomorphism preserve the canonical symplectic form on 𝔸𝕂2​n\mathbb{A}^{2n}_{\mathbb{K}}. In accordance with this, Kontsevich and Kanel-Belov [3] formulated several conjectures on correspondence between automorphisms of the Weyl algebra WnW_{n} and the Poisson algebra PnP_{n} (which is the polynomial algebra 𝕂⁡[x1,…,x2​n]\mathbb{K}[x_{1},\ldots,x_{2n}] endowed with the canonical Poisson bracket) in characteristic zero. In particular, there is a

Conjecture 1.3.

The automorphism groups of the nn-th Weyl algebra and the polynomial algebra in 2​n2n variables with Poisson structure over the rational numbers are isomorphic:

Aut⁡Wn​(ℚ)≃Aut⁡Pn​(ℚ)\Aut W_{n}(\mathbb{Q})\simeq\Aut P_{n}(\mathbb{Q})

Relatively little is known about the case 𝕂=ℚ\mathbb{K}=\mathbb{Q}, and the proof techniques developed in [3] rely heavily on model-theoretic objects such as infinite prime numbers (in the sense of non-standard analysis); that in turn requires the base field 𝕂\mathbb{K} to be of characteristic zero and algebraically closed (effectively ℂ\mathbb{C} by the Lefschetz principle). However, even the seemingly easier analogue of the above conjecture, the case 𝕂=ℂ\mathbb{K}=\mathbb{C}, is known (and positive) only for n=1n=1.

In the case n=1n=1, the affirmative answer to the Kontsevich conjecture, as well as positivity of several isomorphism statements for algebras of similar nature, relies on the fact that all automorphisms of the algebras in question are tame (see definition below). Groups of tame automorphisms are rather interesting objects. Anick [16] has proved that the group of tame automorphisms of 𝕂⁡[x1,…,xN]\mathbb{K}[x_{1},\ldots,x_{N}] is dense (in power series topology) in the subspace of all endomorphisms with non-zero constant Jacobian. This fundamental result enables one to reformulate the Jacobian conjecture as a statement on invertibility of limits of tame automorphism sequences.

Another interesting problem is to ask whether all automorphisms of a given algebra are tame [7, 8, 19, 14, 15]. For instance, it is the case [11] for 𝕂⁡[x,y]\mathbb{K}[x,y], the free associative algebra 𝕂​⟨x,y⟩\mathbb{K}\langle x,y\rangle and the free Poisson algebra 𝕂​{x,y}\mathbb{K}\{x,y\}. It is also the case for free Lie algebras (a result of P.M. Cohn). On the other hand, it is not the case for 𝕂⁡[x,y,z]\mathbb{K}[x,y,z] (the well-known Nagata automorphism, cf. [18, 13]).

While there is reason to expect all polynomial symplectomorphisms – as well as all Weyl algebra automorphisms – to be tame, we are unaware of any conclusive results in this direction. In any case, Anick’s approximation theorem allows one to construct sequences of tame symplectomorphisms for a given polynomial symplectomorphism. The focus of this paper is the problem of lifting of symplectomorphisms: can an arbitrary symplectomorphism in dimension 2​n2n be lifted to an automorphism of the nn-th Weyl algebra in characteristic zero? The lifting problem is the milestone in the Kontsevich conjecture; the use of tame approximation is advantageous due to the fact that we know that tame symplectomorphisms correspond to Weyl algebra automorphisms: in fact [3], the tame automorphism subgroups are isomorphic (when 𝕂=ℂ\mathbb{K}=\mathbb{C}).

In this note we establish the approximation property for polynomial symplectomorphisms, supplying along the way a proof of one of Anick’s approximation results, and comment on the lifting problem. In particular, the main results discussed here are as follows.

Main Theorem 1. Let φ=(φ⁡(x1),…,φ⁡(xN))\varphi=(\varphi(x_{1}),\;\ldots,\;\varphi(x_{N})) be an automorphism of the polynomial algebra 𝕂⁡[x1,…,xN]\mathbb{K}[x_{1},\ldots,x_{N}] over a field 𝕂\mathbb{K} of characteristic zero, such that its Jacobian

J⁡(φ)=det⁡[∂φ⁡(xi)∂xj]\J(\varphi)=\Det\left[\frac{\partial\varphi(x_{i})}{\partial x_{j}}\right]

is equal to 11. Then there exists a sequence {ψk}⊂TAut⁡𝕂⁡[x1,…,xN]\{\psi_{k}\}\subset\operatorname{TAut}\mathbb{K}[x_{1},\ldots,x_{N}] of tame automorphisms converging to φ\varphi in formal power series topology.

Main Theorem 2. Let σ=(σ⁡(x1),…,σ⁡(xn),σ⁡(p1),…,σ⁡(pn))\sigma=(\sigma(x_{1}),\;\ldots,\;\sigma(x_{n}),\;\sigma(p_{1}),\;\ldots,\;\sigma(p_{n})) be a symplectomorphism of 𝕂⁡[x1,…,xn,p1,…,pn]\mathbb{K}[x_{1},\ldots,x_{n},p_{1},\ldots,p_{n}] with unit Jacobian. Then there exists a sequence {τk}⊂TAut⁡Pn​(𝕂)\{\tau_{k}\}\subset\operatorname{TAut}P_{n}(\mathbb{K}) of tame symplectomorphisms converging to σ\sigma in formal power series topology.

Corollary. Let 𝕂=ℂ\mathbb{K}=\mathbb{C} and let σ:Pn​(ℂ)→Pn​(ℂ)\sigma:P_{n}(\mathbb{C})\rightarrow P_{n}(\mathbb{C}) be a symplectomorphism over complex numbers. Then there exists a sequence

ψ1,ψ2,…,ψk,…\psi_{1},\;\psi_{2},\;\ldots,\;\psi_{k},\;\ldots

of tame automorphisms of the nn-th Weyl algebra Wn​(ℂ)W_{n}(\mathbb{C}), such that their images σk\sigma_{k} in Aut⁡Pn​(ℂ)\Aut P_{n}(\mathbb{C}) converge to σ\sigma.

The last proposition is of main concern to us. As we shall see, sequences of tame symplectomorphisms lifted to automorphisms of Weyl algebra (either by means of the isomorphism of [3], or explicitly through deformation quantization Pn​(ℂ)→Pn​(ℂ)​[[ℏ]]P_{n}(\mathbb{C})\rightarrow P_{n}(\mathbb{C})[[\hbar]]) are such that their limits may be thought of as power series in Weyl algebra generators. If we could establish that those power series were actually polynomials, then the Dixmier conjecture would imply the Kontsevich’s conjecture (with ℚ\mathbb{Q} replaced by ℂ\mathbb{C}). Conversely, approximation by tame automorphisms provides a possible means to attack the Dixmier conjecture (and, correspondingly, the Jacobian conjecture). In any case, approximation with respect to power series topology seems to be at the center of these three problems.

2 Endomorphisms of 𝕂⁡[x1,…,xn]\mathbb{K}[x_{1},\ldots,x_{n}], Wn​(𝕂)W_{n}(\mathbb{K}) and Pn​(𝕂)P_{n}(\mathbb{K})

2.1 Definitions and notation

The nn-th Weyl algebra Wn​(𝕂)W_{n}(\mathbb{K}) over 𝕂\mathbb{K} is by definition the quotient of the free associative algebra

𝕂⁡⟨a1,…,an,b1,…,bn⟩\mathbb{K}\langle a_{1},\ldots,a_{n},b_{1},\ldots,b_{n}\rangle

by the two-sided ideal generated by elements

bi​aj−aj​bi−δi​j,ai​aj−aj​ai,bi​bj−bj​bi,b_{i}a_{j}-a_{j}b_{i}-\delta_{ij},\;\;a_{i}a_{j}-a_{j}a_{i},\;\;b_{i}b_{j}-b_{j}b_{i},

with 1≤i,j≤n1\leq i,j\leq n. One can think of Wn​(𝕂)W_{n}(\mathbb{K}) as the algebra

𝕂⁡[x1,…,xn,y1,…,yn]\mathbb{K}[x_{1},\ldots,x_{n},y_{1},\ldots,y_{n}]

with two sets of nn mutually commuting generators (images of the free generators under the canonical projection) which interact according to [yi,xj]=yi​xj−xj​yi=δi​j[y_{i},x_{j}]=y_{i}x_{j}-x_{j}y_{i}=\delta_{ij}, although, unless the context necessitates clarification, we would like to denote the Weyl algebra henceforth by Wn​(𝕂)W_{n}(\mathbb{K}) in order to avoid confusion with 𝕂⁡[X]\mathbb{K}[X] – notation reserved for the ring of polynomials in commuting variables.

The polynomial algebra 𝕂⁡[x1,…,xN]\mathbb{K}[x_{1},\ldots,x_{N}] itself is the quotient of the free associative algebra by the congruence that makes all its generators commutative. When N=2​nN=2n is even, the algebra A2​nA_{2n} carries an additional structure of the Poisson algebra – namely, a bilinear map

{,}:𝕂[x1,…,xN]⊗𝕂[x1,…,xN]→𝕂[x1,…,xN]\{\;,\;\}:\mathbb{K}[x_{1},\ldots,x_{N}]\otimes\mathbb{K}[x_{1},\ldots,x_{N}]\rightarrow\mathbb{K}[x_{1},\ldots,x_{N}]

that turns 𝕂⁡[x1,…,xN]\mathbb{K}[x_{1},\ldots,x_{N}] into a Lie algebra and acts as a derivation with respect to polynomial multiplication. Under a fixed choice of generators, this map is given by the canonical Poisson bracket

{xi,xj}=δi,n+j−δi+n,j.\{x_{i},x_{j}\}=\delta_{i,n+j}-\delta_{i+n,j}.

We denote the pair (𝕂[x1,…,x2​n],{,})(\mathbb{K}[x_{1},\ldots,x_{2n}],\{\;,\;\}) by Pn​(𝕂)P_{n}(\mathbb{K}). In our discussion the coefficient ring 𝕂\mathbb{K} is a field of characteristic zero, and for later purposes (Proposition 4.3) we require 𝕂\mathbb{K} to be algebraically closed. Thus one may safely assume 𝕂=ℂ\mathbb{K}=\mathbb{C} in the sequel.

Throughout we assume all homomorphisms to be unital and preserving all defining structures carried by the objects in question. Thus, by a Weyl algebra endomorphism we always mean a 𝕂\mathbb{K}-linear ring homomorphism Wn​(𝕂)W_{n}(\mathbb{K}) into itself that maps 11 to 11. Similarly, the set End⁡𝕂⁡[x1,…,xn]\End\mathbb{K}[x_{1},\ldots,x_{n}] consists of all 𝕂\mathbb{K}-endomorphisms of the polynomial algebra, while End⁡Pn\End P_{n} is the set of polynomial endomorphisms preserving the Poisson structure. We will call elements of the group Aut⁡Pn\Aut P_{n} polynomial symplectomorphisms, due to the fact that they can be identified with polynomial one-to-one mappings 𝔸𝕂2​n→𝔸𝕂2​n\mathbb{A}^{2n}_{\mathbb{K}}\rightarrow\mathbb{A}^{2n}_{\mathbb{K}} of the affine space 𝔸𝕂2​n\mathbb{A}^{2n}_{\mathbb{K}} which preserve the symplectic form

ω=∑id​pi∧d​xi.\omega=\sum_{i}dp_{i}\wedge dx_{i}.

Any endomorphism φ\varphi of 𝕂⁡[x1,…,xN]\mathbb{K}[x_{1},\ldots,x_{N}], Pn​(𝕂)P_{n}(\mathbb{K}) or Wn​(𝕂)W_{n}(\mathbb{K}) can be identified with the ordered set

(φ⁡(x1),φ⁡(x2),…)(\varphi(x_{1}),\;\varphi(x_{2}),\;\ldots)

of images of generators of the corresponding algebra. For 𝕂⁡[x1,…,xN]\mathbb{K}[x_{1},\ldots,x_{N}] and Pn​(𝕂)P_{n}(\mathbb{K}), the polynomials φ⁡(xi)\varphi(x_{i}) can be decomposed into sums of homogeneous components; this means that the endomorphism φ\varphi may be written as a formal sum

φ=φ0+φ1+⋯,\varphi=\varphi_{0}+\varphi_{1}+\cdots,

where φk\varphi_{k} is a string (of length NN and 2​n2n, respectively) whose entries are homogeneous polynomials of total degree kk.11 1 We set deg⁡xi=1\Deg x_{i}=1. Accordingly, the height ht⁡(φ)\Ht(\varphi) of the endomorphism is defined as

ht⁡(φ)=inf{k|φk≠0},ht⁡(0)=∞.\Ht(\varphi)=\inf\{k\;|\;\varphi_{k}\neq 0\},\;\;\Ht(0)=\infty.

This is not to be confused with the degree of endomorphism, which is defined as deg⁡(φ)=sup{k|φk≠0}\Deg(\varphi)=\sup\{k\;|\;\varphi_{k}\neq 0\}.22 2 For WnW_{n} the degree is well defined, but the height depends on the ordering of the generators. The height ht⁡(f)\Ht(f) of a polynomial ff is defined quite similarly to be the minimal number kk such that the homogeneous component fkf_{k} is not zero. Evidently, for an endomorphism φ=(φ⁡(x1),…,φ⁡(xN))\varphi=(\varphi(x_{1}),\;\ldots,\;\varphi(x_{N})) one has

ht⁡(φ)=inf{ht⁡(φ⁡(xi))| 1≤i≤N}.\Ht(\varphi)=\inf\{\Ht(\varphi(x_{i}))\;|\;1\leq i\leq N\}.

The function

d⁡(φ,ψ)=exp⁡(−ht⁡(φ−ψ))d(\varphi,\psi)=\exp(-\Ht(\varphi-\psi))

is a metric on End⁡𝕂⁡[x1,…,xN]\End\mathbb{K}[x_{1},\ldots,x_{N}]. We will refer to the corresponding topology on End\End (and on subspaces such as Aut\Aut and TAut\operatorname{TAut}) as the formal power series topology.

2.2 Tame automorphisms

We call an automorphism φ∈Aut⁡𝕂⁡[x1,…,xN]\varphi\in\Aut\mathbb{K}[x_{1},\ldots,x_{N}] elementary if it is of the form

φ=(x1,…,xk−1,a​xk+f⁡(x1,…,xk−1,xk+1,…,xN),xk+1,…,xN)\varphi=(x_{1},\ldots,\;x_{k-1},\;ax_{k}+f(x_{1},\ldots,x_{k-1},\;x_{k+1},\;\ldots,\;x_{N}),\;x_{k+1},\;\ldots,\;x_{N})

with a∈𝕂×a\in\mathbb{K}^{\times}. Observe that linear invertible changes of variables – that is, transformations of the form

(x1,…,xN)↦(x1,…,xN)​A,A∈GL⁡(N,𝕂)(x_{1},\;\ldots,\;x_{N})\mapsto(x_{1},\;\ldots,\;x_{N})A,\;\;A\in\GL(N,\mathbb{K})

are realized as compositions of elementary automorphisms.

The subgroup of Aut⁡𝕂⁡[x1,…,xN]\Aut\mathbb{K}[x_{1},\ldots,x_{N}] generated by all elementary automorphisms is the group TAut⁡𝕂⁡[x1,…,xN]\operatorname{TAut}\mathbb{K}[x_{1},\ldots,x_{N}] of so-called tame automorphisms.

Let Pn​(𝕂)=𝕂⁡[x1,…,xn,p1,…,pn]P_{n}(\mathbb{K})=\mathbb{K}[x_{1},\ldots,x_{n},p_{1},\ldots,p_{n}] be the polynomial algebra in 2​n2n variables with Poisson structure. It is clear that for an elementary φ∈Aut⁡𝕂⁡[x1,…,xn,p1,…,pn]\varphi\in\Aut\mathbb{K}[x_{1},\ldots,x_{n},p_{1},\ldots,p_{n}] to be a symplectomorphism, it must either be a linear symplectic change of variables – that is, a transformation of the form

(x1,…,xn,p1,…,pn)↦(x1,…,xn,p1,…,pn)​A(x_{1},\;\ldots,\;x_{n},\;p_{1},\;\ldots,\;p_{n})\mapsto(x_{1},\;\ldots,\;x_{n},\;p_{1},\;\ldots,\;p_{n})A

with A∈Sp⁡(2​n,𝕂)A\in\Sp(2n,\mathbb{K}) a symplectic matrix, or be an elementary transformation of one of two following types:

(x1,…,xk−1,xk+f⁡(p1,…,pn),xk+1,…,xn,p1,…,pn)(x_{1},\;\ldots,\;x_{k-1},\;x_{k}+f(p_{1},\;\ldots,\;p_{n}),\;x_{k+1},\;\ldots,\;x_{n},\;p_{1},\;\ldots,\;p_{n})

or

(x1,…,xn,p1,…,pk−1,pk+g⁡(x1,…,xn),pk+1,…,pn).(x_{1},\;\ldots,\;x_{n},\;p_{1},\;\ldots,\;p_{k-1},\;p_{k}+g(x_{1},\;\ldots,\;x_{n}),\;p_{k+1},\;\ldots,\;p_{n}).

Note that in both cases we do not include translations of the affine space into our consideration, so we may safely assume the polynomials ff and gg to be at least of height one.

The subgroup of Aut⁡Pn​(𝕂)\Aut P_{n}(\mathbb{K}) generated by all such automorphisms is the group TAut⁡Pn​(𝕂)\operatorname{TAut}P_{n}(\mathbb{K}) of tame symplectomorphisms. One similarly defines the notion of tameness for the Weyl algebra Wn​(𝕂)W_{n}(\mathbb{K}), with tame elementary automorphisms having the exact same form as for Pn​(𝕂)P_{n}(\mathbb{K}).

The automorphisms which are not tame are called wild. It is unknown at the time of writing whether the algebras WnW_{n} and PnP_{n} have any wild automorphisms in characteristic zero for n>1n>1, however for n=1n=1 all automorphisms are known to be tame [7, 8, 9, 10]. On the other hand, the celebrated example of Nagata

(x+(x2−y​z)​x,y+2​(x2−y​z)​x+(x2−y​z)2​z,z)(x+(x^{2}-yz)x,\;y+2(x^{2}-yz)x+(x^{2}-yz)^{2}z,\;z)

provides a wild automorphism of the polynomial algebra 𝕂⁡[x,y,z]\mathbb{K}[x,y,z].

It is known due to Kanel-Belov and Kontsevich [3, 4] that for 𝕂=ℂ\mathbb{K}=\mathbb{C} the groups

TAut⁡Wn​(ℂ)​and​TAut​Pn​(ℂ)\operatorname{TAut}W_{n}(\mathbb{C})\;\;\text{and}\;\;\operatorname{TAut}P_{n}(\mathbb{C})

are isomorphic. The homomorphism between the tame subgroups is obtained by means of non-standard analysis and involves certain non-constructible entities, such as free ultrafilters and infinite prime numbers. Recent effort [20, 21] has been directed to proving the homomorphism’s independence of such auxiliary objects, with limited success.

3 Approximation by tame automorphisms

Let φ∈Aut⁡𝕂⁡[x1,…,xN]\varphi\in\Aut\mathbb{K}[x_{1},\ldots,x_{N}] be a polynomial automorphism. We say that φ\varphi is approximated by tame automorphisms if there is a sequence

ψ1,ψ2,…,ψk,…\psi_{1},\;\psi_{2},\ldots,\;\psi_{k},\ldots

of tame automorphisms such that

ht⁡((ψk−1∘φ)​(xi)−xi)≥k\Ht((\psi_{k}^{-1}\circ\varphi)(x_{i})-x_{i})\geq k

for 1≤i≤N1\leq i\leq N and all kk sufficiently large. Observe that any tame automorphism ψ\psi is approximated by itself – that is, by a stationary sequence ψk=ψ\psi_{k}=\psi.

This and the next section are dedicated to the proof of the main results stated in the introduction, which we reproduce here.

Theorem 3.1.

Let φ=(φ⁡(x1),…,φ⁡(xN))\varphi=(\varphi(x_{1}),\;\ldots,\;\varphi(x_{N})) be an automorphism of the polynomial algebra 𝕂⁡[x1,…,xN]\mathbb{K}[x_{1},\ldots,x_{N}] over a field 𝕂\mathbb{K} of characteristic zero, such that its Jacobian

J⁡(φ)=det⁡[∂φ⁡(xi)∂xj]\J(\varphi)=\Det\left[\frac{\partial\varphi(x_{i})}{\partial x_{j}}\right]

is equal to 11. Then there exists a sequence {ψk}⊂TAut⁡𝕂⁡[x1,…,xN]\{\psi_{k}\}\subset\operatorname{TAut}\mathbb{K}[x_{1},\ldots,x_{N}] of tame automorphisms approximating φ\varphi.

Theorem 3.2.

Let σ=(σ⁡(x1),…,σ⁡(xn),σ⁡(p1),…,σ⁡(pn))\sigma=(\sigma(x_{1}),\;\ldots,\;\sigma(x_{n}),\;\sigma(p_{1}),\;\ldots,\;\sigma(p_{n})) be a symplectomorphism of 𝕂⁡[x1,…,xn,p1,…,pn]\mathbb{K}[x_{1},\ldots,x_{n},p_{1},\ldots,p_{n}] with unit Jacobian. Then there exists a sequence {τk}⊂TAut⁡Pn​(𝕂)\{\tau_{k}\}\subset\operatorname{TAut}P_{n}(\mathbb{K}) of tame symplectomorphisms approximating σ\sigma.

Theorem 3.1 is a special case of a classical result of Anick [16] (Anick proved approximation for all étale maps, not just automorphisms). We give here a slightly simplified proof suitable for our context. The second theorem first appeared in [17] and is essential in our approach to the lifting problem in deformation quantization.

The proof of Theorem 3.1 consists of several steps each of which amounts to composing a given automorphism φ\varphi with a tame transformation of a specific type – an operation which allows one to dispose in φ⁡(xi)\varphi(x_{i}) (1≤i≤N1\leq i\leq N) of terms of total degree greater than one and less than a fixed integer kk. Thus the approximating sequence of tame automorphisms is constructed. As was mentioned before, we disregard translation automorphisms completely: all automorphisms discussed here are origin-preserving, so that the polynomials φ⁡(xi)\varphi(x_{i}) have zero free part. This of course leads to no loss of generality.

The process starts with the following straightforward observation.

Lemma 3.3.

There is a linear transformation A∈SL⁡(N,𝕂)A\in\SL(N,\mathbb{K})

(x1,…,xN)↦(x1,…,xN)​A(x_{1},\;\ldots,\;x_{N})\mapsto(x_{1},\;\ldots,\;x_{N})A

such that its composition φA\varphi_{A} with φ\varphi fulfills

ht⁡(φA​(xi)−xi)≥2\Ht(\varphi_{A}(x_{i})-x_{i})\geq 2

for all i∈{1,…,N}i\in\{1,\ldots,N\}.

Proof.

Consider

A1=[∂φ⁡(xi)∂xj]​(0,…,0)A_{1}=\left[\frac{\partial\varphi(x_{i})}{\partial x_{j}}\right]\left(0,\ldots,0\right)

– the linear part of φ\varphi. Its determinant is equal to the value of J⁡(φ)\J(\varphi) at zero, and J⁡(φ)=1\J(\varphi)=1 everywhere. Composing φ\varphi with the linear change of variables induced by A1−1A_{1}^{-1} (on the left) results in an automorphism φA\varphi_{A} that is identity modulo O⁡(x2)\mathit{O}(x^{2}). ∎

Using the above lemma, we may replace φ\varphi with φA\varphi_{A} (and suppress the AA subscript for convenience).

Lemma 3.4.

Suppose that φ∈Aut⁡𝕂⁡[x1,…,xN]\varphi\in\Aut\mathbb{K}[x_{1},\ldots,x_{N}] is identity modulo square terms. Then there exists a set

ρ1,…,ρm\rho_{1},\;\ldots,\;\rho_{m}

of tame automorphisms of degree two such that the composition

ρm∘⋯∘ρ1∘φ=φm\rho_{m}\circ\cdots\circ\rho_{1}\circ\varphi=\varphi_{m}

is identity modulo cubic terms.

Proof.

Suppose that for a fixed generator number ii, the polynomial φ⁡(xi)\varphi(x_{i}) contains a degree-two monomial a​xj​xkax_{j}x_{k}, with jj and kk not equal to ii (jj and kk may coincide). Then the elementary automorphism whose left action kills this term is

xi↦xi−a​xj​xkx_{i}\mapsto x_{i}-ax_{j}x_{k}

(with the rest of the generators unchanged). Applying such transformations several times if needed, we eliminate all degree-two terms in φ⁡(xi)\varphi(x_{i}) with the possible exception of

xi​xj​(for​j≠i)​and​xi2.x_{i}x_{j}\;\;(\text{for}\;j\neq i)\;\;\text{and}\;x_{i}^{2}.

The terms xi​xjx_{i}x_{j} are taken care of by the following transformation

xi↦xi−xi​xj,xj↦xj+12​xi2x_{i}\mapsto x_{i}-x_{i}x_{j},\;x_{j}\mapsto x_{j}+\frac{1}{2}x_{i}^{2}

(again, all other generators are left unchanged). This transform is a two-dimensional automorphism and is therefore tame.

The procedure is then repeated for all ii. In the resulting composite automorphism the only quadratic terms that may occur in the image of xix_{i} are of the form ai​xi2a_{i}x_{i}^{2} for some ai∈𝕂a_{i}\in\mathbb{K}. Since the initial automorphism φ\varphi was identity modulo higher-order terms, and since all transformations performed in the procedure amount to re-scaling the generators (modulo quadratic terms), then the resulting automorphism φm\varphi_{m} will also act as re-scaling modulo higher-order terms. For the Jacobian we then have

J⁡(φm)=c+2​∑i=1Nai​xi+O⁡(x2)\J(\varphi_{m})=c+2\sum_{i=1}^{N}a_{i}x_{i}+\mathit{O}(x^{2})

On the other hand, as generator re-scaling is a (tame) automorphism, its Jacobian is constant. Together with the initial assumption J⁡(φ)=1\J(\varphi)=1 (recall that the Jacobian of a composition of mappings is the product of Jacobians of these mappings) this implies that the Jacobian for the resulting automorphism is constant. That in turn forces the coefficients aia_{i} to be zero, and we are done.33 3 To be precise, we are done after we re-scale the generators once again, so that the resulting φm\varphi_{m} is identity modulo cubic terms. ∎

Lemma 3.5.

Suppose that, given an automorphism φ\varphi with unit Jacobian, we can, by composing it on the left with tame automorphisms, transform it into the automorphism φm\varphi_{m}:

φm​(xi)=xi+Qi,ht⁡(Qi)≥m+1.\varphi_{m}(x_{i})=x_{i}+Q_{i},\;\;\Ht(Q_{i})\geq m+1.

Then we can find a tame automorphism ρ\rho such that

ρ∘φm​(xi)=xi+Si,ht⁡(Si)≥m+2.\rho\circ\varphi_{m}(x_{i})=x_{i}+S_{i},\;\;\Ht(S_{i})\geq m+2.
Proof.

Let qi≠0q_{i}\neq 0 denote the degree mm homogeneous part of QiQ_{i}. By acting on the left with elementary transformations, we may make qiq_{i} (in the resulting automorphism) divisible by xix_{i}. Let us call any monomial in qiq_{i} that is not divisible by xi2x_{i}^{2} marked.

For any marked monomial, if j,kj,\;k are such that the monomial contains xjx_{j} and xkx_{k} with degree one, let us perform an elementary transformation

xj↦(xj+xk)/2,xk↦(xj−xk)/2.x_{j}\mapsto(x_{j}+x_{k})/\sqrt{2},\;\;x_{k}\mapsto(x_{j}-x_{k})/\sqrt{2}.

This change of variables decomposes the monomial into two, each of which is of the form described in two cases below.

We now are going to eliminate the marked monomials as follows.

First case: the monomial is of the form a​xi​xjmax_{i}x_{j}^{m}. Such monomials are eliminated by the following two-dimensional (and therefore tame) automorphism

xi↦xi−a​xi​xjm,xj↦xj+a​xim+1m+1.x_{i}\mapsto x_{i}-ax_{i}x_{j}^{m},\;\;x_{j}\mapsto x_{j}+a\frac{x_{i}^{m+1}}{m+1}.

Second case: the monomial is of the form −a​xi​xjbj​xkbk​f-ax_{i}x_{j}^{b_{j}}x_{k}^{b_{k}}f with ff not containing xix_{i}, xjx_{j} or xkx_{k}. We may assume

1≤bj≤bk,  2≤bk,1\leq b_{j}\leq b_{k},\;\;2\leq b_{k},

otherwise we use elementary transformations. Consider now the following four types of automorphisms:

xj↦xj+xi​xkbk,x_{j}\mapsto x_{j}+x_{i}x_{k}^{b_{k}},
xi↦xi+abj+1​xjbj+1​f,x_{i}\mapsto x_{i}+\frac{a}{b_{j}+1}x_{j}^{b_{j}+1}f,
xj↦xj−xi​xkbk,x_{j}\mapsto x_{j}-x_{i}x_{k}^{b_{k}},

and

xi↦xi−abj+1​xjbj+1​f.x_{i}\mapsto x_{i}-\frac{a}{b_{j}+1}x_{j}^{b_{j}+1}f.

It is straightforward to check that after a consecutive left action by these transformations the marked monomial −a​xi​xjbj​xkbk​f-ax_{i}x_{j}^{b_{j}}x_{k}^{b_{k}}f vanishes, while other changes in monomial composition of QiQ_{i} amount to adding to xjx_{j} a monomial −abj+1​xjbj+1​xkbk​f-\frac{a}{b_{j}+1}x_{j}^{b_{j}+1}x_{k}^{b_{k}}f, which lowers the overall number of marked monomials by one.

At this point we make the following remark, which is left as a simple exercise to the reader. Let

σ1=(x1+a​x2n,x2,…,xn)\sigma_{1}=(x_{1}+ax_{2}^{n},\;x_{2},\;\ldots,\;x_{n})

and

σ2=(x1,x2+a​x1l,…,xn)\sigma_{2}=(x_{1},\;x_{2}+ax_{1}^{l},\;\ldots,\;x_{n})

be two automorphisms. Their commutator is then

σ0=σ2−1∘σ1−1∘σ2∘σ1=(x1−a​b​n​x2n−1​x1l+A⁡(x1,x2),x2+a​b​l​x2n​x1l−1+B⁡(x1,x2),x3,…,xn),\sigma_{0}=\sigma_{2}^{-1}\circ\sigma_{1}^{-1}\circ\sigma_{2}\circ\sigma_{1}=\\ (x_{1}-abnx_{2}^{n-1}x_{1}^{l}+A(x_{1},x_{2}),\;x_{2}+ablx_{2}^{n}x_{1}^{l-1}+B(x_{1},x_{2}),\;x_{3},\;\ldots,\;x_{n}),

where ht⁡A,ht⁡B>l+n−1\Ht A,\;\Ht B>l+n-1.

Now, for our automorphism, consider the Jacobian in the form44 4 We suppress the superscript indicating the transformed automorphism for convenience and in order to avoid any confusion.

J=∂φ⁡(x1)∂x1​…​∂φ⁡(xN)∂xN+R,\J=\frac{\partial\varphi(x_{1})}{\partial x_{1}}\ldots\frac{\partial\varphi(x_{N})}{\partial x_{N}}+R,

where RR denotes the remainder of the expression for the determinant of a matrix as a polynomial in its entries. Note that each monomial in RR contains at least two non-diagonal entries of the Jacobian matrix. By our assumption, each non-diagonal entry is of height at least mm. Therefore,

ht⁡R>2​m≥m+2\Ht R>2m\geq m+2

for m≥2m\geq 2 (the quadratic case m=1m=1 was discussed in the previous lemma). This implies

J=1+∂Q1∂x1+⋯+∂QN∂xN+R1,\J=1+\frac{\partial Q_{1}}{\partial x_{1}}+\cdots+\frac{\partial Q_{N}}{\partial x_{N}}+R_{1},

where R1R_{1} is the sum of the remaining monomials. In particular, ht⁡R1>m+2\Ht R_{1}>m+2.

Let uu be a monomial in Q1Q_{1} which is not equal to x1m+1x_{1}^{m+1}. Then there is a number jj such that QjQ_{j} has the monomial vv:

∂u∂x1=a​∂v∂xj.\frac{\partial u}{\partial x_{1}}=a\frac{\partial v}{\partial x_{j}}.

Now, using a pair of tame automorphisms as in the remark above (corresponding to x1x_{1}, xjx_{j} and their degrees in uu and in vv respectively, with suitable coefficients), we eliminate uu in Q1Q_{1}. Reiterated, such a procedure eliminates all monomials of degree less than (m+1)(m+1) in QiQ_{i}, with the possible exception of ai​xim+1a_{i}x_{i}^{m+1}. Since

∂q1∂x1+⋯+∂qN∂xN=0,\frac{\partial q_{1}}{\partial x_{1}}+\cdots+\frac{\partial q_{N}}{\partial x_{N}}=0,

and, on the other hand,

∂qi∂xi=ci​xim\frac{\partial q_{i}}{\partial x_{i}}=c_{i}x_{i}^{m}

the conclusion is that ci=0c_{i}=0 for all ii, which means that all monomials of degree (m+1)(m+1) are eliminated. The lemma is proved. ∎

The last lemma concludes the proof of Theorem 3.1.

4 Approximation by tame symplectomorphisms and lifting to Weyl algebra

We turn to the proof of the more relevant to our context Theorem 3.2. on symplectomorphism approximation. The strategy is completely analogous to the proof of approximation for polynomial automorphisms with unit Jacobian, therefore we supply a brief walk-through and leave it to the interested reader to fill in the details.

The first lemma of the preceding proof now takes the following form.

Lemma 4.1.

There is a linear transformation A∈Sp⁡(2​n,𝕂)A\in\Sp(2n,\mathbb{K})

(x1,…,xn,p1,…,pn)↦(x1,…,xn,p1,…,pn)​A(x_{1},\;\ldots,\;x_{n},\;p_{1},\;\ldots,\;p_{n})\mapsto(x_{1},\;\ldots,\;x_{n},\;p_{1},\;\ldots,\;p_{n})A

such that its composition σA\sigma_{A} with σ\sigma fulfills

ht⁡(σA​(xi)−xi)≥2,ht⁡(σA​(pi)−pi)≥2\Ht(\sigma_{A}(x_{i})-x_{i})\geq 2,\;\;\Ht(\sigma_{A}(p_{i})-p_{i})\geq 2

for all i∈{1,…,n}i\in\{1,\ldots,n\}.

Moving forward, consider the situation

σ⁡(xi)=xi+Ui+Ui′,σ⁡(pi)=pi+Vi+Vi′,\sigma(x_{i})=x_{i}+U_{i}+U^{\prime}_{i},\;\;\sigma(p_{i})=p_{i}+V_{i}+V^{\prime}_{i},

with

deg⁡Ui=deg⁡Vi=k,Ui​Vi≠0,deg⁡Ui′>k,deg⁡Vi′>k,k>1.\Deg U_{i}=\Deg V_{i}=k,\;\;U_{i}V_{i}\neq 0,\;\;\Deg U^{\prime}_{i}>k,\;\;\Deg V^{\prime}_{i}>k,\;\;k>1.
Lemma 4.2.

In the situation as above, we can, using tame automorphisms, eliminate all monomials of degree kk.

Proof.

The fact that σ\sigma preserves the Poisson bracket implies, as may be checked directly, the equality

∑i=1n(∂Ui∂xi+∂Vi∂pi)=0.\sum_{i=1}^{n}\left(\frac{\partial U_{i}}{\partial x_{i}}+\frac{\partial V_{i}}{\partial p_{i}}\right)=0.

Observe also that we may perform transformations which are similar to all changes of variables we introduced in the proof of the previous theorem.

Let k=2k=2. Then, performing variable changes similar to the quadratic case of the previous theorem, we reduce UiU_{i} and ViV_{i} to

Ui=ai​xi2,Vi=bi​pi2.U_{i}=a_{i}x_{i}^{2},\;\;V_{i}=b_{i}p_{i}^{2}.

The requirement

σ∗​(∑id​pi∧d​xi)=∑id​pi∧d​xi\sigma^{*}\left(\sum_{i}dp_{i}\wedge dx_{i}\right)=\sum_{i}dp_{i}\wedge dx_{i}

then implies ai=bi=0a_{i}=b_{i}=0.

For k>2k>2 we again, after performing elementary transformations, arrive at

Ui=ai​xik,Vi=bi​pikU_{i}=a_{i}x_{i}^{k},\;\;V_{i}=b_{i}p_{i}^{k}

which again implies ai=bi=0a_{i}=b_{i}=0. This proves the lemma, and with it the theorem. ∎

Once the approximation for the case of symplectomorphisms has been established, we can investigate the problem of lifting symplectomorphisms to Weyl algebra automorphisms. More precisely, one has the following

Proposition 4.3.

Let 𝕂=ℂ\mathbb{K}=\mathbb{C} and let σ:Pn​(ℂ)→Pn​(ℂ)\sigma:P_{n}(\mathbb{C})\rightarrow P_{n}(\mathbb{C}) be a symplectomorphism over complex numbers. Then there exists a sequence

ψ1,ψ2,…,ψk,…\psi_{1},\;\psi_{2},\;\ldots,\;\psi_{k},\;\ldots

of tame automorphisms of the nn-th Weyl algebra Wn​(ℂ)W_{n}(\mathbb{C}), such that their images σk\sigma_{k} in Aut⁡Pn​(ℂ)\Aut P_{n}(\mathbb{C}) approximate σ\sigma.

Proof.

This is an immediate corollary of Theorem 3.2 and the existence of tame subgroup isomorphism [3].

∎

A few comments are in order. First, the deformation quantization of elementary symplectomorphisms is a very simple procedure: one need only replace the xix_{i} and pip_{i} by their counterparts x^i\hat{x}_{i} and p^i\hat{p}_{i} in the Weyl algebra WnW_{n}. Because the transvection polynomials ff and gg (in the expressions for elementary symplectomorphisms) depend, as has been noted, on one type of generators (resp. pp and xx), the quantization is well defined.

Second, as the tame automorphism groups TAut⁡Wn​(ℂ)\operatorname{TAut}W_{n}(\mathbb{C}) and TAut⁡Pn​(ℂ)\operatorname{TAut}P_{n}(\mathbb{C}) are isomorphic, the correspondence between sequence of tame symplectomorphisms converging to symplectomorphisms and sequences of tame Weyl algebra automorphisms is one to one. The main question is how one may interpret these sequences as endomorphisms of Wn​(ℂ)W_{n}(\mathbb{C}).

Our construction shows that these sequences of tame automorphisms may be thought of as (vectors of) power series – that is, elements of

ℂ​[[x^1,…,x^n,p^1,…,p^n]]2​n.\mathbb{C}[[\hat{x}_{1},\ldots,\hat{x}_{n},\hat{p}_{1},\ldots,\hat{p}_{n}]]^{2n}.

The main problem therefore consists in verifying that these vectors have entries polynomial in generators – that is, that the limits of lifted tame sequences are Weyl algebra endomorphisms.

5 Conclusion

We have developed tame approximation theory for symplectomorphisms in formal power series topology. By virtue of the known correspondence between tame automorphisms of the even-dimensional affine space and tame automorphisms of the Weyl algebra, which is the object corresponding to the affine space in terms of deformation quantization, we have arrived at the lifting property of symplectomorphisms. This line of research may yield new insights into endomorphisms of the Weyl algebra, the Dixmier conjecture, and the Jacobian conjecture.
